body.text: Australia’s push for greater production of critical minerals and green steel overlooks a resource that is already above ground: scrap metal, much of which we still ship offshore unprocessed. The country needs a policy to maximise domestic supply of this material.

Steelmaking is shifting towards electric arc furnaces, which run largely on scrap and made about 30 percent of the world’s crude steel in 2025. Scrap is becoming a resource for which countries are competing.

This is a national security issue. Defence production, from shipbuilding to armoured vehicles and military-base construction, depends on a reliable supply of steel, and Australia’s supply is concentrated in big plants based around iron-producing blast furnaces. Concentration invites attack, or at least disruption. In September, the government ruled out funding a restart of Whyalla’s 60-year-old blast furnace, leaving BlueScope’s Port Kembla works with the country’s only operating iron-making blast furnace.

Electric arc furnaces are, in effect, recycling plants. They are smaller and can be far more numerous and dispersed, which makes supply from them more resilient. Plants with similar characteristics can be used for other metals.

The volumes are large. Australia exported 2.55 million tonnes of ferrous scrap in 2025–26, according to the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water. That was the most in any year since at least 2017–18. The Australian Steel Institute estimates that each year, more than 1 million tonnes of these exports is unprocessed scrap from old cars and whitegoods. It still carries plastics, glass and tyres that would be illegal to export on their own. The institute expects local mills to need another 500,000 tonnes of scrap a year within three years.

The institute wants exports of unprocessed scrap steel banned. But a ban would be the wrong tool. It would hand a few domestic buyers a captive supply. It would push down the prices paid to collectors and small yards, giving them less reason to recover metal at all. And it would do nothing for copper and aluminium, where most of the value lies.

Non-ferrous metals are a bigger prize. They made up only 16 percent of Australia’s scrap exports by weight in 2025–26 but 67 percent by value: A$3.05 billion out of A$4.58 billion. Copper scrap, about 113,000 tonnes, alone earned A$1.23 billion. Aluminium scrap earned A$1.43 billion. A tonne of copper scrap was worth about 18 times more than a tonne of ferrous scrap. China alone took about a third of the non-ferrous value, followed by India and South Korea.

Copper and aluminium are both on the government’s Strategic Materials List. Yet neither that list nor the Critical Minerals Strategy mentions the copper and aluminium already sitting in old cables, cars, buildings and machinery. Bringing that metal back into use takes far less energy than making it new: recycled aluminium, for example, needs about 95 percent less. A country that calls these metals strategic but ships their scrap away without a plan has a gap in its thinking.

A better policy would start with data. The government tracks scrap exports by metal and destination but publishes little on how much scrap of each grade is generated and processed at home. Without that, no one can say how much domestic supply a policy could unlock.

Next comes processing capacity. Waste glass, plastics, tyres and paper must already be processed before they can be exported. The same rules could be extended to unprocessed car and white-goods scrap. That would keep it at home for shredding and sorting. Processed scrap could still be exported where local mills couldn’t use it all: exports are about five times the extra scrap the institute expects local mills to need. But as local electric arc furnace capacity grows, more of it would stay here.

The Recycling Modernisation Fund, which shares the cost of new recycling plants with state governments and industry, has focused mainly on glass, plastics, tyres and paper. Opening it to metal would help pay for shredders and sorting lines. For copper and aluminium, the missing piece is local remelting and refining, so that high-grade scrap becomes metal here rather than overseas.

Finally, high-grade scrap needs a place in the policies now focused on primary metals. These include the strategic materials list, the green metals measures in Future Made in Australia and plans for a new electric arc furnace at Whyalla. Recovered steel, copper and aluminium should count as supply in their own right.

Australia treats the minerals in the ground as strategic assets and the metal above it as something to ship. As steelmakers compete for scrap and defence planners look for resilience, that distinction makes less sense every year.
